query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of a reactive element (e.g., 5–10 at.% Cu) to the CoCrFeNi matrix will promote the in-situ formation of a continuous, lubricious oxide glaze during sliding that adapts across a wide temperature range, thereby maintaining low friction and reduced wear from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix with homogeneous microstructure but limited ability to keep low friction and wear at high temperatures.
generation.intervention: Minor alloying addition of a reactive element (such as Cu) into the CoCrFeNi system.
generation.conditions: Dry sliding wear tests in ambient air conducted over temperatures ranging from ~25 °C to 800 °C, under typical loads (e.g., 5–30 N) and sliding speeds encountered in tribological evaluations.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a nano-engineered, continuous oxide glaze layer at the sliding interface.
generation.mechanism: During sliding, the Cu addition preferentially oxidizes to form a dense and adherent oxide layer. At lower temperatures, this layer smoothens contact asperities and reduces adhesive wear, while at elevated temperatures the oxide layer becomes more reactive and resistant to plastic deformation, thus sustaining a low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the temperature ramp.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy, the Cu-alloyed variant is expected to exhibit a more stable and lower friction coefficient as well as a decreased wear rate over the full test temperature range.
generation.baseline: The plain CoCrFeNi alloy, which has difficulty maintaining low friction and wear, particularly at higher temperatures due to abrasive and oxidative wear mechanisms.
generation.boundary: Effectiveness is evaluated under dry sliding conditions in air, with temperatures spanning from room temperature (~25 °C) to 800 °C and under sliding loads typically between 5–30 N; the intervention’s benefit is limited to these conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal reactive element type and concentration, as well as the long-term reliability and cyclic stability of the oxide glaze under extended thermal and mechanical cycling, need further detailed investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of baseline CoCrFeNi alloy and another with 5–10 at.% Cu addition. Subject both to identical dry sliding wear tests over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C under controlled load (e.g., 10 N) and sliding speed conditions. Monitor friction behavior in situ and conduct post-test surface analyses (e.g., SEM and EDS) to assess the formation and continuity of the oxide glaze.
measurements: Wear rates quantified as volume loss per normal load and sliding distance
Surface morphology and composition of the sliding interface (via SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cu-alloyed samples do not show a statistically significant reduction and stabilization in the friction coefficient and wear rate across the entire temperature range compared to the baseline, or if a continuous lubricious oxide glaze does not form on the Cu-alloyed samples, the hypothesis is considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

cited_evidence.text: The rise in CoF with a higher load applied during the wear test as illustrated in Fig. 6a–e is due to increased contact pressure at the interface. With the increase in load, the sliding parts were pressed against each other and it resulted in higher pressure at the interface. More resistance is offered by the counterparts during sliding owing to a higher pressure which results in higher friction at higher loads. Additionally, the soft matrix around the reinforcement easily wears out at higher loads which in turn results in contact between reinforcement protrusions and hard counterpart. This sliding of two harder phases results in a higher coefficient of friction. The CoF values increase considerably with an increase in sliding velocity as depicted in Fig. 7a–e. There is a chance of mechanically mixed layer formation at the sliding interface when parts are sliding at lower velocities. The presence of a mechanically mixed layer serves to prevent direct contact between sliding components, resulting in the lower CoF.
